reasoning: The existing skill already covers answer slots, clue relations, and conventional naming, so I avoided adding another generic rule. I retained the narrower incident-clue distinction, qualified title-language guidance to follow the clue and substantive evidence, and combined direct-answer qualifiers and ellipsis handling into one replacement of the clue-echo text. The protected section is untouched. Each edit is supported by one of the two source patches. [optimizer-ranked: selected 2/3 edits]

edits.target: For proper names and titles, use the conventional form that identifies the requested entity. Do not substitute a nickname or later brand name for the historically relevant label, omit words from a work's title when the work is requested, or add optional middle names. Conversely, when the clue requests a generic class, do not embellish it with a narrower associated name.
edits.content: When a work has original-language and translated or market titles, use the form the clue requests. If the clue or reliable context explicitly identifies the original-language title and asks for the work without specifying a release-language title, use that original title; use the translation when the clue asks for the English or release title. If neither form is signaled, follow the conventional title supported by context rather than assuming one.

edits.target: In noisy or search-style context, a passage may repeat the clue without supplying its answer. Treat that echo as a locator for relevant material, not as evidence for the missing answer; use substantive passages to identify the target and verify distinctive clue details. If the passage explicitly pairs the clue with an answer, it can serve as direct evidence.
edits.content:
In noisy or search-style context, a passage may repeat the clue without supplying its answer. Treat that echo as a locator for relevant material, not as evidence for the missing answer; use substantive passages to identify the target and verify distinctive clue details. If the passage explicitly pairs the clue with an answer, it can serve as direct evidence. Preserve the complete answer label and any qualifier that is part of the requested or canonical name, rather than shortening it merely because the referent is clear.

When a quoted fragment begins with an ellipsis, consider whether preceding text has been omitted. If context identifies the phrase, supply the missing prefix rather than the visible tail or a work associated with it. Apply this only when the ellipsis marks omitted text; a trailing or stylistic ellipsis is not a blank.

Edit 2 adds a useful rule for recognizing omitted prefixes in ellipsis-led quotations, though its answer-label reminder largely duplicates existing guidance. Edit 0 overlaps substantially with the existing type and quotation/relation rules.
